questions.prompt: What do two SVCHOST.EXE .pf files with different hash suffixes indicate?
options: The executable ran from two different paths, since the hash is derived from the full path -- only one of which is System32
The file was executed on two different dates
questions.explanation: This single property -- the hash encodes the path, not the file -- is what turns an unremarkable listing into a masquerading finding.

questions.prompt: Which SVCHOST.EXE entry is the anomalous one, and why?
options: The one with 1,104 runs, because that volume is abnormal
The one with a run count of 1, executing 41 seconds after Word launched PowerShell
Neither; svchost always has multiple entries
questions.explanation: Legitimate svchost.exe runs constantly, so 1,104 executions is expected. A single execution inside the suspicious time cluster is the outlier.

questions.prompt: What makes the 09:14:22 to 09:15:03 window significant?
options: WINWORD, POWERSHELL, and the anomalous SVCHOST all executed within 41 seconds -- a sequence rather than a coincidence
Prefetch only records events in 60-second windows
All three entries have identical run counts
questions.explanation: Temporal clustering across three otherwise unrelated executables is what links them into a single chain worth investigating.

questions.prompt: What should be extracted from the two SVCHOST .pf files next?
options: The referenced-file lists, which give the actual directory each ran from and what each touched in its first ten seconds
questions.explanation: PECmd recovers the referenced-file list, which is often the only surviving record of a since-deleted binary's behavior.
